tips.title: Same signs subtract, opposite signs add
tips.body: Once one letter has **matching coefficients**, look at the signs. **Same sign → subtract** the equations. **Opposite signs → add** them. Getting this the wrong way round leaves the letter you were trying to remove.

tips.title: Substitute into the other equation
tips.body: Find both values, then put them into the equation you did **not** use to find the second one. If it balances, the pair is right. Checking in the same equation you just solved proves nothing.

tips.title: Two unknowns need two equations
tips.body: One equation with two letters has infinitely many solutions — $x + y = 10$ is true for $(1,9)$, $(2,8)$ and endlessly more. It takes a **second** equation to pin down one pair, which is why they are solved *simultaneously*.

tips.title: Scale one or both to make a match
tips.body: If no coefficient matches, multiply one or both equations through so that one letter does. Multiply **every term**, including the number on the right — forgetting that term is the commonest slip in the method.

tips.title: On a graph, the solution is the crossing point
tips.body: Two linear equations are two straight lines, and the solution is where they **cross**. That is why there is normally exactly one answer, and it makes a graph a fair way to find an approximate solution when a question asks for one.

why.matters:
One equation with two unknowns does not have an answer. It has a **line** of them — swap a pound off the coffee onto the tea and the bill still comes to the same total.

A second equation, as long as it is genuinely new information rather than the first one rescaled, cuts that line down to a single point. That is the whole idea, and it is why the method is worth more than the algebra: **two unknowns need two independent measurements**, three need three, and no amount of cleverness gets round it.

Once you see that shape you start seeing it everywhere. Almost anything described as "working out what we cannot measure directly, from several things we can" is this.

examples.title: The prices nobody put on the bill
examples.body:
Two rounds at the same café. The first was 3 coffees and 2 teas for £11.40. The second was 2 coffees and 3 teas for £10.60.

Neither receipt shows a single price. You can still work both out.

Scale the first by 3 and the second by 2, so both have 6 teas: £34.20 and £21.20. Subtract, and every tea cancels: 5 coffees cost £13.00, so a coffee is £2.60 and a tea is £1.80.

What happened there is worth more than the answer. Two numbers you could never observe were recovered from two numbers you could, and the trick was arranging for one unknown to cancel. Stock control, splitting a shared bill, working out a unit cost from invoices and reading a utility bill backwards from two months of totals are all the same move.

props.title: Scaling until the teas match, then subtracting

visual.alt: A table showing two cafe rounds scaled so that both contain six teas and then subtracted, leaving five coffees costing thirteen pounds

examples.title: How a phone knows where it is
examples.body:
A satellite tells your phone one thing: how far away it is. One distance puts you somewhere on a sphere around it, which is no use. Two distances narrow it to a circle of possible places. Three cut that down to a point.

Draw it flat and it is easy to see. Each station gives a circle of places you could be. Two circles cross at **two** points, so two measurements still leave a genuine wrong answer on the table. The third circle is what throws it away.

That is simultaneous equations with the same rule as the café bill: one equation for each unknown. Position on a map is two unknowns, so it takes three distances rather than two, because these equations are circles and circles meet twice.

Satellite navigation needs 4, not 3. The fourth is there because your phone's clock is not accurate enough, so the time is a fourth unknown — and a fourth unknown needs a fourth equation.

steps.title: Why two equations
steps.body:
**One equation with two unknowns has no single answer.** Take

$$x + y = 10$$

This is satisfied by $(1, 9)$, by $(2, 8)$, by $(4.5, 5.5)$ and by infinitely many other pairs. Nothing in the equation picks one of them out.

**Add a second equation and that changes.** If also

$$x - y = 4$$

then only **one** pair satisfies **both** at once. Solving them *simultaneously* means finding the pair that works in both.

**The graphical picture makes this obvious.** Each linear equation is a **straight line**, and every point on that line is a solution of it. Two lines normally **cross exactly once**, and that crossing point is the pair that lies on both — the simultaneous solution.

That also tells you when things go differently. **Parallel lines never meet**, so such a pair has **no solution**; and if the two equations are really the same line, every point on it works.

**The spec asks for both routes**: solving **algebraically**, which is exact, and finding **approximate solutions using a graph**. The algebra is what most questions want, but the graph is what explains it.

steps.title: When a coefficient already matches
steps.body:
**The method is elimination: get rid of one letter, solve for the other, then come back.**

If one letter already has the **same coefficient** in both equations, you can eliminate it straight away.

**Same signs → subtract. Opposite signs → add.**

That rule is worth saying out loud each time, because doing it the wrong way round doubles the letter you were trying to remove.

steps.title: Turning a situation into equations
steps.body:
**Spec point A21 asks you to translate a situation into equations, solve them, and interpret the answer.** Those are three separate jobs and the marks are split across them.

**A worked example in words.** Three coffees and two teas cost £11. One coffee and two teas cost £7. What does each cost?

1. **Define the letters, in writing.** Let $c$ be the cost of a coffee in pounds and $t$ the cost of a tea. Stating this is worth a mark and makes the rest readable.
2. **Write one equation per sentence**:

$$3c + 2t = 11$$
$$c + 2t = 7$$

3. **Solve.** The $t$ terms match with the same sign, so subtract: $2c = 4$, giving $c = 2$. Then $2 + 2t = 7$, so $t = 2.5$.
4. **Interpret, in the units of the question.** A coffee costs **£2** and a tea **£2.50**.

**That last step is a real mark.** An answer of *c = 2, t = 2.5* has solved the algebra but not answered the question, which asked about money.

**Check against the original words, not just the equations.** Three coffees and two teas: $3 \times £2 + 2 \times £2.50 = £11$ ✓. This catches a mistranslation, which the algebra itself cannot — if you wrote the equations wrongly, solving them correctly still gives the wrong answer.

steps.body:
**Part A.**

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say the rule before you act on it.** Once a letter has matching coefficients: **same sign, subtract; opposite signs, add**. Done the wrong way round, the letter you meant to remove **doubles** instead of vanishing, and the mistake is usually spotted three lines later. Saying which you are doing and why costs nothing.

**Multiply every term when scaling.** Doubling $2x + 3y = 12$ gives $4x + 6y = \mathbf{24}$, not $4x + 6y = 12$. Leaving the right-hand side alone is the single most common error in the method, and the resulting answer looks perfectly plausible.

**Check in the equation you did not use.** After finding $x$, you substitute into one equation to get $y$ — so that equation is **guaranteed** to balance and tests nothing. The **other** equation is the real check. Checking in both is better still.

**The graph explains the exceptions.** Two lines that **cross once** give one solution. **Parallel** lines — same gradient, different intercept — never meet, so the pair has **no solution**, and algebraically you will find both letters vanishing to leave something false like $0 = 7$. If the two equations describe the **same line**, everything cancels to $0 = 0$ and every point on the line works. Recognising what those outcomes mean is worth more than being puzzled by them.

**In a worded problem, the translation is the examined skill.** Define the letters **in writing**, write one equation per sentence, and finish by **interpreting** the answer in the units asked for. *c = 2* is not an answer to a question about money; **a coffee costs £2** is.

**And check a worded answer against the words.** Substituting into your own equations tests only your algebra. If the equations were wrong, the algebra will be flawlessly wrong — only the original situation can catch that.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **One equation with two unknowns** has infinitely many solutions; a **second** equation pins down one pair.
- Each linear equation is a **straight line**, and the solution is where the lines **cross**.
- The spec asks for both **algebraic** solutions and **approximate** ones from a graph.
- The method is **elimination**: remove one letter, solve for the other, then substitute back.
- If a letter already has **matching coefficients**: **same sign → subtract**, **opposite signs → add**.
- If nothing matches, **scale one or both equations** so that one letter does.
- **Multiply every term**, including the number on the right — the commonest error in the method.
- Choose whichever letter needs the **smaller multipliers**; it need not be $x$.
- Having found one value, **substitute** it into the simpler equation to get the other.
- **Check in the equation you did not use** — the one you used is guaranteed to balance.
- **Parallel lines** mean **no solution**, and the algebra collapses to something false such as $0 = 7$.
- Two equations describing the **same line** give $0 = 0$ and infinitely many solutions.
- For a **worded problem**: **define the letters in writing**, write **one equation per sentence**, solve, then **interpret** in the right units.
- **Check a worded answer against the original words**, because a mistranslation survives a check against your own equations.

questions.prompt: Explain why a pair of simultaneous equations is needed to find two unknowns, describe how elimination works, and explain what it means graphically when there is no solution.
questions.solution:
A single equation with two unknowns cannot be solved on its own because **infinitely many pairs satisfy it**. $x + y = 10$ is true for $(1, 9)$, $(2, 8)$, $(4.5, 5.5)$ and endlessly many others — nothing in the equation singles one out. Adding a **second** equation changes that: normally only **one pair** satisfies both at once, and finding it is what solving *simultaneously* means.

The usual method is **elimination**: get rid of one letter so that a single equation in a single unknown remains.

First, get one letter to have **matching coefficients** in both equations. Sometimes it already does. If not, **multiply one or both equations through** until it does — and multiply **every term**, including the number on the right-hand side. Forgetting that number is the commonest error in the whole method, because the answer it produces still looks plausible.

Then apply the rule: **same signs, subtract; opposite signs, add**. In $3x + 2y = 16$ and $x + 2y = 8$ the $y$ terms are $+2y$ in both, so subtracting gives $2x = 8$ and $x = 4$. In $4x + y = 13$ and $2x - y = 5$ the $y$ terms are opposite, so adding gives $6x = 18$ and $x = 3$. Getting the rule backwards **doubles** the letter you were trying to remove.

With one value found, **substitute it back** into the simpler equation to find the other. Then **check in the equation you did not use** — the one you substituted into is guaranteed to balance and tests nothing.

Graphically, each equation is a **straight line**, and every point on a line satisfies its equation. The solution is therefore the point lying on **both** lines: their **crossing point**. That is why there is normally exactly one answer.

It also explains the exception. Two lines with the **same gradient but different intercepts** are **parallel** and never meet, so the pair has **no solution**. Algebraically this shows up unmistakably: both letters vanish and you are left with something false, such as $0 = 7$. That is a genuine result rather than a mistake. And if the two equations describe the **same line**, everything cancels to $0 = 0$, meaning every point on that line is a solution.

Describes elimination: match a coefficient, add or subtract according to the signs, solve, then substitute back.
States the rule: same signs subtract, opposite signs add.
Explains that parallel lines never cross, so there is no solution, and the algebra produces a false statement.

questions.prompt: Three coffees and two teas cost £11. One coffee and two teas cost £7. Set up and solve a pair of simultaneous equations to find the cost of each, showing how you would check your answer.
questions.solution:
First, **define the letters** in writing. Let $c$ be the cost of a coffee in pounds, and $t$ the cost of a tea in pounds. This is worth doing explicitly — it is worth a mark, and everything that follows is unreadable without it.

Now **translate one sentence at a time**. Three coffees and two teas cost £11 gives

$$3c + 2t = 11$$

and one coffee and two teas cost £7 gives

$$c + 2t = 7$$

The $t$ terms are **$+2t$ in both** — matching coefficients with the **same sign** — so the equations are **subtracted**:

$$(3c - c) + (2t - 2t) = 11 - 7$$

which gives $2c = 4$, so $c = 2$.

**Substitute back** into the simpler equation: $2 + 2t = 7$, so $2t = 5$ and $t = 2.5$.

**Interpret the answer in the units the question used.** A coffee costs **£2** and a tea costs **£2.50**. Stopping at *c = 2, t = 2.5* has completed the algebra but not answered a question about money, and that final translation carries a mark of its own.

For the **check**, there are two things worth doing, and they are not the same. Substituting into the equation I did not use tests the algebra: $3(2) + 2(2.5) = 6 + 5 = 11$ ✓.

But the more valuable check is against the **original words**: three coffees at £2 and two teas at £2.50 come to £6 + £5 = **£11**, and one coffee and two teas come to £2 + £5 = **£7**. Both sentences are satisfied.

That second check matters because it tests something the first cannot. Substituting into my **own** equations only confirms my arithmetic — if I had translated the sentences wrongly, my answer would fit those wrong equations perfectly and the check would still pass. Only going back to the situation itself can catch a mistranslation.

**Substitute back** into the simpler equation: $2 + 2t = 7$, so $2t = 5$ and $t = 2.5$.

**Interpret the answer in the units the question used.** A coffee costs **£2** and a tea costs **£2.50**. Stopping at *c = 2, t = 2.5* has completed the algebra but not answered a question about money, and that final translation carries a mark of its own.

For the **check**, there are two things worth doing, and they are not the same. Substituting into the equation I did not use tests the algebra: $3(2) + 2(2.5) = 6 + 5 = 11$ ✓.

But the more valuable check is against the **original words**: three coffees at £2 and two teas at £2.50 come to £6 + £5 = **£11**, and one coffee and two teas come to £2 + £5 = **£7**. Both sentences are satisfied.

That second check matters because it tests something the first cannot. Substituting into my **own** equations only confirms my arithmetic — if I had translated the sentences wrongly, my answer would fit those wrong equations perfectly and the check would still pass. Only going back to the situation itself can catch a mistranslation.

examTechnique.body:
The method is short and the errors are predictable. Match a coefficient, apply **same signs subtract, opposite signs add**, solve, substitute back, and check in the **other** equation.

When scaling, multiply **every** term. When the question is in words, **define the letters**, write one equation per sentence, and finish by saying what the answer means in the units asked for.
examinerErrors: Adding when the signs **match**, or subtracting when they are **opposite**.
Scaling an equation but leaving the **number on the right** unchanged.
Checking in the equation just used, which is guaranteed to balance.
Treating $0 = 7$ as an arithmetic slip rather than as **no solution**.
Forgetting to **define the letters** in a worded problem.
Leaving a worded answer as *x = 2* rather than **£2**.
Losing a sign when subtracting: $-4y - (-4y)$ is $0$, not $-8y$.
Solving for one letter and forgetting to find the other.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states the sign rule **before** using it, and says which equation it is checking in and why the other one would prove nothing. It scales by multiplying **every** term, and picks whichever letter needs the **smaller** multipliers rather than defaulting to $x$. It recognises $0 = 7$ as **parallel lines with no solution** and $0 = 0$ as the same line twice, instead of assuming a mistake. On a worded problem it **defines the letters**, **interprets** the answer in the right units, and checks against the **original sentences** — knowing that a check against its own equations would pass even if the translation were wrong.
